before.name: the plan
before.label: before the essay
before.text: George Eastman invented the user. Not the camera, which existed, and not flexible film, which cost him five million dollars to be told he had not invented. What he built in 1888 was a customer who had never existed: an ordinary person, with no chemistry and no darkroom, who could keep a piece of their own life. *You press the button, we do the rest.* It was the first true consumer company in America, and the promise was so complete that the man behind it disappeared into it. He removed himself from the product, from his gifts, from his own authorized biography, and finally from the world, on a March afternoon in 1932, with the alternative covered and a second pistol in the bookcase. The company he left ran on his instructions for eighty years without the judgment that wrote them. It gave the United States its eyes over the Soviet Union, put the first photograph of the Earth in front of humanity, and then, in a single year, 1976, invented the digital image, patented the sensor every phone now carries, licensed it out to the world, and chose to collect rent instead of build. It died as the man it began by firing: George Selden, the patent attorney who held paper instead of making things. In 2012 the last roll came off a machine that had run a hundred and one years, and the arsenal built to cover every avenue was sold to Apple and Google for a fifth of asking. Kodak was the only monument Eastman had. He had no children and no heirs; four biographies were commissioned by his own company and none was allowed out; the one he authorized he edited himself, and it ends in ascending triumph because it was published two years before he shot himself. Now the company is gone as well, and what survives is a slide in a business school deck about an incumbent too stupid to see digital coming, which is not what happened. This book is the first honest accounting of him, and it can only be written now, because the image has finally left matter altogether. No lens, no light, no referent. Development brought out what light had already written; the models bring out what was never there. Same verb, same dark. For the first time since 1888 the arc is complete, and you can stand at the end of the thing Eastman started and see all of it, including the parts he arranged for you not to see.

before.name: the outline
before.label: before the essay
before.text: This book is the first honest accounting of the man who started it, and it can only be written now. Eastman spent his life binding the photograph to matter: to silver, to gelatin, to film. That argument has just finally lost. Images now arrive with no lens, no light, and no moment that happened, summoned out of static. Photography's oldest technical term for the picture hiding in an undeveloped negative is the *latent image*. The term for the space these new pictures are pulled from is *latent space*. Same word, same dark, a hundred and forty years apart. Development brought out what light had already written. The models bring out what was never there.
